intro: Music is your language, and you hear it more and more from the inside. You live in Vienna among patrons, publishers and friends, in a world built for listeners, and you have to rework how you compose, talk and earn a living.

tunnel.why: Communication: from about 1818 every talk goes through paper and the conversation books.

market.why: Stage and public life: after 1814 deafness ended his career as a performing pianist.

office.why: Courts: the guardianship fight over his nephew took years of hearings.

bridge.why: Patrons: Archduke Rudolph, Lobkowitz and Kinsky guaranteed his income in 1809.

quiet.why: Inner ear: he sketched at home and composed the late works from imagination.

advantage.title: The inner ear
advantage.text: Beethoven composed late works from his inner ear and planned whole structures in his head. Up to three times, a question you know well counts as answered.

life.title: Bonn, 1770
life.text: Ludwig is baptised in Bonn on 17 December 1770 into a family of court musicians. His father Johann trains him hard on the keyboard, hoping to present him as a child prodigy.

life.title: A household to hold together
life.text: Johann drinks, and money is short. After Ludwig's mother dies in 1787 he plays and works as an organist, and he soon becomes the main provider for his younger brothers.

life.title: To Vienna, 1792
life.text: Ludwig moves to Vienna, studies with Joseph Haydn and is soon admired as a pianist and improviser. Nobles such as Prince Lichnowsky give him rooms, money and a stage.

life.title: The first sign
life.text: Success is arriving when something starts to change.

q.q: What did Beethoven first notice around 1798?
q.x: Around 1798, aged 27, he began to hear ringing and buzzing in his ears. His hearing then faded over the following years.

life.title: Hiding it from patrons
life.text: He fears that a musician who cannot hear will lose patrons, pupils and concerts. So he keeps quiet and avoids parties, which makes him look unfriendly. Nobody around him has any tools for deafness.

life.title: The Heiligenstadt letter, 1802
life.text: Content note: despair. In a letter to his brothers that he never sent, Ludwig writes about shame, isolation and thoughts of dying. He says his art held him back, and he went on to compose for 25 more years.

life.title: A new, bolder sound
life.text: He writes the Third Symphony (the Eroica, 1804), the Fifth with its four-note opening, and the opera Fidelio. Publishers and patrons keep paying for music that sounds like nothing before it.

life.title: New ways to talk
life.text: By about 1818 he can hardly hear speech at all.

q.q: How did visitors talk with the almost-deaf Beethoven?
a: They wrote in his conversation books
They spoke into a speaking tube
q.x: Friends wrote their half of the conversation in notebooks; he answered aloud. Many of these books survive and show his daily life, and he also tried ear trumpets.

life.title: Walls, courts and debt
life.text: Concert halls and salons were designed only for listening. Beethoven also fights for custody of his nephew Karl through the courts from 1815 to 1820, with strained money and health. Few friends can talk with him easily.

life.title: The Ninth, 1824
life.text: The Ninth Symphony, with its choral Ode to Joy, premieres in Vienna on 7 May 1824. At the end a singer turns Beethoven around so he can see the audience cheering and waving, since he cannot hear the applause.

life.title: The late quartets
life.text: In his last years he writes string quartets that surprise later composers. They come from what he calls his inner hearing, with friends and copyists who put the score into readable form.

life.title: Vienna, 1827
life.text: Beethoven dies on 26 March 1827, aged 56. Many thousands of people line the streets for his funeral. Today he is played everywhere, and the Ode to Joy melody of his Ninth is the anthem of the European Union.

flags: Birth date is not documented; only the baptism on 17 December 1770 is, so the text says baptised.
Custody fight dates (1815 to 1820) are widely cited; check precise end date.
Funeral crowd is often given as 10,000 to 20,000; text says 'many thousands'.
The Ninth is the source of the EU anthem melody (arranged by Karajan); text simplifies this.
The Heiligenstadt Testament was addressed to his brothers and never sent, which is the standard account.

evidence.ev: In the Heiligenstadt Testament he wrote that his hearing had been failing for years and that it had pushed him to withdraw from people.
He used conversation books: visitors wrote their side of a talk, he answered aloud.
His last public appearance as a pianist in a new work was in 1814; after that his hearing no longer let him perform on stage.
After his brother died he fought in the Vienna courts for guardianship of his nephew Karl, a case that cost him years and money.
Archduke Rudolph and two princes promised him a yearly income so he would stay in Vienna and keep composing.
He kept sketchbooks and heard music in his head; the late quartets and the Ninth were written deaf.
